how-much-should-i-set-aside-for-gig-driv.text:
← Gig driver net pay calculator

How much to set aside for gig driving taxes

DoorDash, Uber Eats, Instacart, Uber, and Lyft pay drivers as independent contractors. No app withholds federal income tax, state income tax, or self-employment tax from a payout the way an employer withholds from a paycheck. Whatever a driver does not set aside during the year is due, in full, at tax time — or sooner, if quarterly estimated payments are required.

This page will not hand you a percentage. The right reserve depends on filing status, state, total income from every source, deductions, and whether you owe quarterly estimates — none of which a free calculator can know, and picking a number for you would be a claim about what you owe rather than arithmetic on what you typed. What it can do is show you what a percentage you supply actually removes from a session.

Worked example. A session nets $149.36 in profit after vehicle cost (gross pay minus gas, maintenance, and a share of insurance). At a 25% reserve, that holds back $37.34, leaving $112.02 — about $18.67/hour on a 6-hour session, down from $24.89/hour before the reserve. The reserve never touches a losing session: if vehicle cost had exceeded gross pay, the reserve would be $0 and take-home would equal the loss, not a smaller loss plus a phantom refund.

Two things this reserve deliberately does not do:

  1. It does not model quarterly due dates or underpayment penalties — it is a running tally of what one session should have set aside, not a filing calendar. For the actual IRS safe-harbor payment and the real (holiday-adjusted) due dates, see the quarterly estimated tax calendar.
  2. It does not net against other income, other jobs, or last year's refund. Whether a slow week's loss offsets something else is a judgement for your return, not this page.

Open the calculator, put in your own reserve percentage, and see what it does to your next session before you spend the gross number. Nothing is uploaded.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not tax, financial, or legal advice. It does not replace a qualified tax preparer. Verify every figure and your actual tax obligation before relying on it. The authors accept no liability for loss arising from its use.

index.html.text:
FOR DOORDASH, UBER EATS, INSTACART, UBER & LYFT DRIVERS

Gross pay isn’t take-home pay.

The app screen shows what it paid you per hour. It never subtracts gas, tires, oil changes, or insurance — those are entirely yours. Enter one session’s gross pay, miles, and hours, and see what you actually kept per hour and per mile, plus what to set aside for taxes nobody withholds for you.

This session

Whatever period you want to check — one dash, one shift, one week. Count every mile the car moved, including the drive to go online and the drive home.

Your vehicle (per mile)

Maintenance/mile is your own reserve for oil changes, tires, and repairs — not the IRS standard mileage rate, which changes every year and would go stale here. Prefer the current standard rate as one figure? Put it here and set gas price to 0.

Monthly fixed cost

Insurance and other fixed costs don’t care how many sessions you drove this month. This session gets the share of them its miles represent, out of your typical monthly business miles.

Tax reserve, and how this session compares

Nothing withholds tax for a self-employed driver. Put in whatever share of profit you set aside for self-employment and income tax and every figure below accounts for it. Leave it at 0 and the page behaves exactly as if the reserve did not exist. We do not guess the percentage — ask a tax preparer for yours.

What this checks

Every delivery and rideshare app shows gross pay per hour or per trip. None of them subtract the car. The decision a driver actually faces is whether this session, after gas and wear, still cleared what it looked like it cleared on the app screen — and what is left once a tax reserve comes out too. How much to set aside for gig-driving taxes walks through the reserve in search-query words.

It does not tell you which platform to drive for, which order to accept, or what your car is worth. The gap between gross pay and net pay is arithmetic on the numbers you typed.

Deciding on a single offer before you accept it? Is this order worth taking? prices one offer's payout, miles and minutes after the car and finds the lowest payout that meets your floor.

Already using the Gridwise app to track pay and mileage over time? See how this one-session calculator differs from Gridwise's ongoing, account-linked tracking. Wondering why the number here differs from the app's own gross-per-hour figure? See this calculator vs. the app's own earnings screen.

Common questions

How do I calculate my real hourly pay driving for DoorDash, Uber Eats, or Instacart?

Take everything the app paid out this session — base pay, tips, promotions — and subtract what the vehicle actually cost to run: fuel for every mile driven (including the drive to go online and back home), a per-mile reserve for maintenance and tires, and a share of your monthly insurance and other fixed costs spread across your typical monthly mileage. Divide what is left by hours logged, not by hours with a delivery in progress. On this page’s starting figures — $180 gross, 90 miles, 6 hours, 28 MPG, $3.49 gas — the vehicle costs about $30.64 for the session, so $30.00/hour gross becomes about $24.89/hour net, before income tax.

What miles count toward the cost, active delivery miles or every mile?

Every mile the car moved this session, not just miles with an order in progress. The drive to a good starting spot, the loop between orders with nothing assigned, and the drive home all burn the same gas and put the same wear on the car as an active mile does. Undercounting miles by only logging active-delivery mileage understates vehicle cost and overstates how much the session actually netted.

How much should I set aside for taxes as a DoorDash, Uber, or Instacart driver?

This page will not tell you a percentage — that depends on your filing status, state, total income, deductions, and quarterly-estimate schedule, and picking one for you would be a claim about what you owe. What it does is arithmetic once you tell it your own reserve percentage: it holds that share out of session profit only (never out of a losing session, which reserves nothing), and shows both the pre-tax profit and what is actually left after the reserve. Ask a tax preparer for your percentage, then use this page to see what it does to a session’s take-home.

Am I actually making minimum wage after gas and car costs?

Enter an hourly wage to compare against — a state minimum wage, a job offer, whatever you want to check against — and the page reports the gap between that number and this session’s net-per-hour, both stated before income tax so they compare on the same basis. It does not assume a minimum wage for you; wages vary too much by state and city to guess at one.

Does this use the IRS standard mileage rate?

No. The standard mileage rate is a single blended figure the IRS sets once a year for a tax deduction, and it changes annually — hardcoding a specific year’s rate here would go stale the first time it changed. This page instead asks for your own gas price, MPG, and a maintenance reserve per mile, plus your monthly insurance and other fixed costs spread across your typical monthly miles, so the cost per mile reflects your actual car rather than a national average. If you prefer to use the current standard mileage rate as a single per-mile figure, put it in the maintenance-per-mile box and set gas price to 0.

What gross pay do I need to hit a take-home goal?

Type an hourly take-home goal and the page solves backwards: it takes the session’s vehicle cost, adds the profit needed to clear that goal after the tax reserve, and reports the gross pay — and gross pay per mile — that would take. At the starting figures with a 25% tax reserve, a $20/hour take-home goal on a 6-hour, 90-mile session solves to about $190.64 of gross pay, roughly $2.12 per mile.

Is this order worth taking?

The offer screen shows a payout and a distance. It does not show what the miles cost, how long you will wait at the restaurant, or the empty drive afterwards. Type what the offer says and what you expect, and see what it pays per hour and per mile after the car, and the lowest payout that meets your own floor.

Only fuel and upkeep, the costs that grow with each mile, are charged to an offer. Insurance and phone plan are owed either way; the session calculator spreads them across a whole shift. Want a tax reserve too? How much to set aside. Have a full trip export? The earnings report analyzer shows which app, weekday and hour pay best.

Common questions

Is this delivery order worth taking?

Divide what it pays after the car by the time it really takes, from the moment you accept to the moment you are free for the next offer. Count the drive to the pickup, the wait at the restaurant, the drive to the customer, and any empty drive back to a busy area. Example: a $7.50 offer that is 3 miles to the customer, 2.5 miles to the restaurant and 2.5 miles back, 33 minutes in all, costs about $1.56 in fuel and wear at 28 MPG, $3.49 gas and 7 cents a mile for upkeep. That is $10.81 an hour after the car, not the $13.64 the app’s pay-per-hour suggests. For an $18 an hour floor, the offer would have to pay at least $11.46.

What is the minimum payout I should accept per mile?

There is no right figure, only your own. The page solves it: type the net-per-hour and net-per-mile floors you want and it reports the lowest payout that clears both for the distance and time of that offer. Whichever floor is stricter sets the number.

Why doesn't this count my insurance and phone plan?

Those are owed whether you accept the offer or not, so they do not change the choice between accepting and declining. Only fuel and wear, which grow with every mile, are charged to an offer. The session calculator on the main page spreads fixed costs across a whole shift to answer a different question: what the shift netted.

Should I count the drive back?

If the drop-off is in a zone where offers come quickly, enter 0 miles and minutes back. If you will have to drive somewhere else before the next offer, that drive is part of this order, and leaving it out is the usual way an offer looks better than it was.

This calculator vs. the Gridwise app

Gridwise is a phone app built for ongoing tracking: create a driver account, link your Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart, or other gig-platform account so it can auto-import earnings, and it runs background GPS tracking to log mileage over days and weeks. Its effective-hourly figure is built from that tracked history — gross earnings minus logged mileage and expenses — and deeper analytics sit behind a paid Gridwise Plus tier that starts with a 14-day trial and then bills automatically unless cancelled.

That makes Gridwise the right choice for tracking pay and mileage automatically across every trip, every app, over time. This page answers a narrower, faster question: for one session you already have numbers for, right now, what did the car actually cost, and what's really left — with no account, no install, and nothing uploaded.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's my average effective hourly rate across weeks of dashes, tracked automatically? Gridwise's linked-account tracking.
For this one session, what did the car cost at my own gas price and MPG, and what's left per hour and per mile? This calculator — type the session's numbers, get an answer immediately, nothing installed.
What should I set aside for self-employment tax on this session's profit? This calculator's tax reserve figure — enter your own reserve percentage.
What gross pay would this session need to hit a take-home goal? This calculator's target take-home solver. Gridwise's public materials describe forward tracking, not a reverse solver for a take-home goal.
Can I check the number without creating an account or installing anything? This calculator — a static page, no sign-up, no app store.

This tool needs no account and no gig-platform link: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your gross pay, miles, and every other figure stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere, and a shareable link carries your inputs after the # in the URL rather than on a server.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or the Gridwise app?

Both answer different questions. Gridwise is a phone app: you create a driver account, link your Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, or Instacart account so it can auto-import earnings, and it runs background GPS tracking to log mileage over days and weeks, building an ongoing effective-hourly and expense history. This page is a single static form: no account, no download, no linking a gig platform. You type one session's gross pay, miles, hours, gas price, MPG, and a maintenance-per-mile reserve, and it computes that session's net pay per hour and per mile, a self-employment tax reserve, and the gross pay needed to hit a take-home goal — right now, with nothing installed and nothing uploaded.

Does Gridwise compute the same vehicle-cost breakdown this page does?

Not the same way. Gridwise's own material describes its effective-hourly figure as gross earnings minus logged mileage and expenses, drawn from its background GPS tracking and whatever expenses a driver has entered in the app — a rolling average built from tracked data, not a single session priced against a specific gas price and MPG you choose. This page asks for your own gas price, MPG, and a maintenance-per-mile reserve for one session, plus monthly insurance and other fixed costs prorated across your typical monthly mileage, so the figure is arithmetic you can check against a fuel receipt and your own odometer for that one session.

Is Gridwise free?

The core tracking is free to use, but a driver account is required and deeper analytics sit behind Gridwise Plus, a paid tier that starts with a 14-day trial and then bills automatically unless cancelled. This calculator has no account, no trial, and nothing that bills — it is a free static page with no server behind the numbers you type.

Is this page affiliated with Gridwise?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Gridwise, Inc. Gridwise is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is for.

vs-the-apps-earnings-screen.html.text:
← Gig driver net pay calculator

This calculator vs. the app's own earnings screen

Every gig platform's earnings screen does the same arithmetic: base pay plus tips plus promotions, added up and divided by the hours you were online, into one gross-per-hour figure. It is fast, and it is the authoritative record of what a session actually paid out.

What it has no field for is the car. Gas, tires, oil changes, and insurance are entirely the driver's own cost, and no platform subtracts them before showing a per-hour number -- it has no way to know your gas price, your MPG, or what your insurance actually costs. So "I made $33.85 an hour" on the earnings screen and "I kept $33.85 an hour" get treated as the same sentence when they usually are not.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What did this session pay out -- base pay, tips, promotions? The app's own earnings screen -- the authoritative record, and this calculator does not replace it.
What did the car actually cost this session, at my own gas price and MPG? This calculator -- type the session's numbers, get an answer immediately, nothing installed.
What should I set aside for self-employment tax on what's left? This calculator's tax reserve figure -- enter your own reserve percentage.
What gross pay would this session need to hit a take-home goal? This calculator's target take-home solver -- the earnings screen has no reverse solver.
Can I check the number without creating an account or linking a platform? This calculator -- a static page, no sign-up, nothing linked.
Run one session's numbers now

A worked example, computed from this calculator's own arithmetic: a session pays $220 for 95 miles and 6.5 hours online. The earnings screen would show $33.85 an hour. Pricing the vehicle at this session's own gas price (28 MPG, $3.40/gallon), an 8-cent per-mile maintenance reserve, and $145 a month in insurance and other fixed costs prorated across 1,400 typical monthly miles brings the vehicle cost to $28.98 for this session, leaving $29.39 an hour before tax. A 25% self-employment tax reserve on that profit brings what's actually kept to $22.04 an hour -- $11.81 less than the $33.85 the earnings screen displayed, a 35% gap the screen never shows.

This tool needs no account and no gig-platform link: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your gross pay, miles, and every other figure stay on this device -- nothing is uploaded anywhere, and a shareable link carries your inputs after the # in the URL rather than on a server.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or the app's own earnings screen?

Both, for different numbers. The app's earnings screen is the fastest way to see what a session paid out -- base pay, tips, and promotions, added up and divided by the hours you were online. It is also the authoritative record of what was actually paid, and this calculator does not try to replace it. What the earnings screen has no field for is the vehicle: gas, wear on tires and the engine, and insurance are entirely the driver's own cost, and none of those platforms subtract them before showing a per-hour figure. This calculator takes that same session's gross pay, miles, and hours and prices the car on top of it, plus a self-employment tax reserve, so the number it shows is what actually stayed in the driver's pocket rather than what the app paid out.

Why doesn't the app's earnings screen subtract vehicle cost itself?

Because the platform has no way to know it. Gas price, fuel economy, how a driver's own car wears, and what insurance actually costs are figures no gig platform has access to -- they vary by driver, by car, and by week, and the app only knows what it paid out, not what a driver spent to earn it. A per-hour figure that never subtracts a cost the platform cannot see is not wrong, exactly; it is answering a narrower question than "what did I keep."

How big is the gap between gross pay per hour and what actually stays?

A worked example, computed from this calculator's own arithmetic: a session pays $220 for 95 miles and 6.5 hours online. The app's earnings screen would show $33.85 an hour. This session's own gas price (28 MPG at $3.40/gallon), an 8 cent per mile maintenance reserve, and $145 a month in insurance and other fixed costs prorated across 1,400 typical monthly miles price the vehicle at $28.98 for this session, leaving $29.39 an hour before tax. A 25% self-employment tax reserve on that profit brings it to $22.04 an hour actually kept -- $11.81 less than the $33.85 the app displayed, a 35% gap the earnings screen never shows.

Does this calculator track earnings automatically across sessions?

No. It prices one session at a time, from the numbers you type in -- no account, no linked gig-platform login, and no background tracking. That is a real trade: an app that links your accounts and logs mileage automatically saves the typing, at the cost of an account and, on some platforms, a paid tier for the deeper breakdown. This calculator is the other trade -- nothing to sign up for, and an answer as soon as you have one session's numbers to type in.

Also: How much should I set aside for gig driving taxes? and this calculator vs. the Gridwise app, for automatic tracking across sessions.
